GPU Automatic Differentiation Options for Julia (2025)

Executive Summary

Current recommendation for Powerful.jl: Continue using CPU autodiff with ForwardDiff.jl for Jacobian computation, even for GPU-based systems.

Reasoning:

  • GPU autodiff ecosystem is still immature in Julia (as of 2025)
  • CPU Jacobian computation is fast enough (~107ms for 135k variables)
  • Newton solvers converge in 3-5 iterations, so total overhead is acceptable
  • Manual GPU kernels for residuals are already very fast

Available GPU Autodiff Packages

1. Enzyme.jl (Most Promising, But Experimental)

Official site: https://enzyme.mit.edu/julia/

Type: Reverse-mode AD (can also do forward-mode)

GPU Support Status (2025):

  • ✅ Technically works - First fully automatic AD tool to differentiate GPU kernels
  • ⚠️ Highly experimental - CUDA support still in active development
  • ⚠️ Complex setup - Requires careful module architecture for cross-device differentiation
  • ✅ Supports both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs

Key Features:

  • LLVM-based compiler plugin (source-to-source transformation)
  • Can differentiate existing CUDA kernels directly
  • Best CPU performance among all Julia AD packages
  • Supports both forward and reverse mode

How It Works:

using Enzyme, CUDA

# Can differentiate GPU kernels directly
function gpu_kernel!(output, input)
    i = threadIdx().x + (blockIdx().x - 1) * blockDim().x
    if i <= length(output)
        @inbounds output[i] = f(input[i])
    end
    return nothing
end

# Enzyme can compute gradients
autodiff(Reverse, gpu_kernel!, Duplicated(output, d_output),
         Duplicated(input, d_input))

Limitations:

  1. Mutation handling - Requires careful handling of mutating operations
  2. Type stability - More sensitive to type instabilities than ForwardDiff
  3. LLVM module complexity - Cross-device differentiation requires workarounds
  4. Learning curve - More complex API than ForwardDiff
  5. Documentation - Less mature than ForwardDiff

Performance (when it works):

  • Best CPU performance among Julia AD packages
  • GPU performance unknown for large sparse Jacobians
  • Designed more for optimization (scalar objectives) than Jacobians

Maturity: ⭐⭐☆☆☆ (2/5 - Experimental for GPU)

Recommendation for Powerful.jl:

  • Wait - Too experimental for production use
  • Monitor - Track development, especially with new Reactant.jl integration
  • Consider for optimization - If you add optimal power flow later

2. Reactant.jl + Enzyme (Emerging, Very Promising)

Official site: https://github.com/EnzymeAD/Reactant.jl

Type: XLA-based compilation with Enzyme integration

Status (2025):

  • ✅ Most reliable and fastest for NVIDIA GPUs (according to recent benchmarks)
  • ⚠️ NVIDIA-only - No AMD support yet
  • ⚠️ New package - Released recently, still maturing

How It Works:

using Reactant

# Compiles Julia functions to MLIR → XLA → GPU
@reactant function my_computation(x)
    # Your Julia code here
    # Automatically compiled for GPU
    # Enzyme used for differentiation
end

Key Features:

  • Compiles Julia to MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation)
  • Uses XLA (Accelerated Linear Algebra) backend
  • Automatic optimization and fusion
  • Built-in Enzyme support for AD
  • Targets CPU, GPU (NVIDIA), and TPU

Advantages:

  • High-level interface (less manual kernel writing)
  • Aggressive optimizations via XLA
  • Best performance for GPU (when compatible)

Limitations:

  1. NVIDIA-only - Requires CUDA, no AMD support
  2. Very new - Limited production battle-testing
  3. Subset of Julia - Not all Julia features supported
  4. Compilation overhead - First run can be slow

Maturity: ⭐⭐⭐☆☆ (3/5 - Promising but new)

Recommendation for Powerful.jl:

  • Watch closely - This is the future direction
  • Experiment - Try on small test cases
  • Not production-ready yet - Wait for more maturity

3. Zygote.jl (Mature, But Not Ideal for GPU Kernels)

Official site: https://fluxml.ai/Zygote.jl/

Type: Reverse-mode AD via source-to-source transformation

GPU Support:

  • ✅ Works with GPU arrays - CuArray support
  • ⚠️ Slow deprecation - Being phased out in favor of Enzyme
  • ⚠️ Not designed for kernels - Better for high-level operations

Key Features:

  • Mature and widely used in ML community
  • Best GPU support among "traditional" Julia AD packages (excluding Reactant)
  • Automatic differentiation of high-level array operations

How It Works:

using Zygote, CUDA

x = cu(rand(1000))
y = cu(rand(1000))

# Can differentiate high-level operations on GPU arrays
gradient(x -> sum(x .* y .^ 2), x)

Advantages:

  • Most mature GPU AD (besides Reactant)
  • Works well with ML frameworks (Flux.jl)
  • Good for high-level array operations

Limitations:

  1. Not for custom kernels - Doesn't differentiate CUDA kernel code
  2. Mutation restrictions - No in-place operations
  3. Being deprecated - Ecosystem moving to Enzyme
  4. Buggy - Known reliability issues
  5. Performance - Not optimized for scientific computing

Maturity: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆ (4/5 - Mature but deprecated)

Recommendation for Powerful.jl:

  • No - Not suitable for custom GPU kernels
  • Wrong tool - Designed for ML, not scientific computing
  • Avoid - Ecosystem is moving away from Zygote

4. ForwardDiff.jl (Current Solution, CPU-Only)

Official site: https://github.com/JuliaDiff/ForwardDiff.jl

Type: Forward-mode AD

GPU Support:

  • ❌ CPU-only - No GPU support
  • ✅ Can compute Dual numbers on CPU and use with CPU solvers

Key Features:

  • Most mature AD package in Julia
  • Excellent performance for Jacobians (many outputs from many inputs)
  • Rock-solid reliability
  • Easy to use

Performance for Power Systems:

  • IEEE 14 (28 vars): 9 μs
  • IEEE 39 (78 vars): 18 μs
  • ACTIVSg 70k (135,800 vars): 107 ms

Advantages:

  1. Rock solid - Production-ready, well-tested
  2. Best for Jacobians - Forward-mode is optimal for sparse Jacobians
  3. Easy to use - Simple API, good documentation
  4. Mature sparse coloring - Excellent integration with SparseDiffTools

Limitations:

  • CPU-only (no GPU execution)
  • For dense problems with many inputs, reverse-mode would be faster

Maturity: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (5/5 - Production-ready)

Recommendation for Powerful.jl:

  • Current choice - Keep using this
  • Fast enough - 107ms for 135k variables is acceptable
  • Reliable - No surprises, works every time

Practical Strategies for GPU + Autodiff

Strategy 1: Hybrid CPU/GPU (Current Approach) ✅ RECOMMENDED

What:

  • Compute residuals on GPU (fast, 1.5ms for 135k vars)
  • Transfer state to CPU
  • Compute Jacobian with ForwardDiff on CPU (107ms)
  • Transfer back and solve linear system on GPU

Performance:

70k-bus system:
  GPU residual:        1.5 ms  ⚡
  Data transfer:       ~1 ms
  CPU Jacobian:      107.0 ms
  Total per Newton:  ~110 ms
  Newton iterations:   3-5
  Total solve:       ~400 ms

Advantages:

  • ✅ Works today
  • ✅ Reliable (ForwardDiff is rock-solid)
  • ✅ Fast enough for most applications
  • ✅ GPU accelerates residuals (biggest bottleneck in time-stepping)

Disadvantages:

  • ⚠️ Data transfer overhead (~1-2ms)
  • ⚠️ Can't leverage GPU for Jacobian computation

When to use: Always - This is the best approach right now

Strategy 2: Pure CPU with Sparse Coloring ✅ ALSO GOOD

What:

  • Everything on CPU
  • Use sparse ForwardDiff with matrix coloring
  • Excellent for systems up to ~500k variables

Performance:

70k-bus system (CPU-only):
  Residual:          1.6 ms
  Jacobian:        107.0 ms
  Total per Newton: ~109 ms

Advantages:

  • ✅ Simple - No CPU/GPU data movement
  • ✅ Reliable
  • ✅ Less memory usage
  • ✅ Portable (no GPU required)

Disadvantages:

  • ⚠️ Residuals slower than GPU (but only ~1ms difference)
  • ⚠️ Less scalable for very large systems

When to use:

  • Systems < 100k buses
  • No GPU available
  • Simplicity preferred over maximum performance

Strategy 3: Manual Analytical Jacobian on GPU (Future Option)

What:

  • Hand-code analytical Jacobian formulas
  • Implement as GPU kernels
  • Maximum performance, maximum effort

Estimated Performance:

70k-bus system:
  GPU residual:        1.5 ms
  GPU Jacobian:       ~5 ms (estimated)
  Total per Newton:   ~7 ms
  Speedup vs CPU:    15x

Advantages:

  • ✅ Maximum performance
  • ✅ No CPU/GPU transfer
  • ✅ Full control

Disadvantages:

  • ❌ High development cost (months of work)
  • ❌ Maintenance burden
  • ❌ Error-prone (must match residual code)
  • ❌ Less flexible (hard to change models)

When to use:

  • Only for >1M variable systems
  • Only if Jacobian is the bottleneck (unlikely)
  • Only if you have time to implement and validate

Strategy 4: Wait for Reactant.jl (Future)

What:

  • Wait 1-2 years for Reactant.jl to mature
  • Migrate code to Reactant when ready
  • Get automatic GPU compilation + AD

Advantages:

  • ✅ Best of both worlds (GPU + AD)
  • ✅ Less manual kernel writing
  • ✅ Automatic optimizations

Disadvantages:

  • ⏳ Not ready yet (2025)
  • ⚠️ May require code refactoring
  • ⚠️ NVIDIA-only

When to use: Keep monitoring, experiment on side projects

Recommended Path Forward for Powerful.jl

Short Term (2025)

Continue using ForwardDiff.jl on CPU:

  1. ✅ Works reliably today
  2. ✅ Performance is acceptable (107ms for 135k vars)
  3. ✅ Zero code changes needed
  4. ✅ Can still use GPU for residual evaluation

Optimization opportunities:

  • Cache workspace (already done ✅)
  • Use sparse coloring (already done ✅)
  • Parallelize with threads (minor gain)

Medium Term (2026)

Experiment with Reactant.jl:

  1. Create proof-of-concept on small test cases
  2. Benchmark against current approach
  3. Evaluate code refactoring effort
  4. Decision point: Migrate or stay with ForwardDiff

Long Term (2027+)

Options:

  1. If Reactant works well: Migrate to Reactant + Enzyme
  2. If current approach sufficient: Stick with ForwardDiff
  3. If need extreme performance: Consider manual analytical Jacobian

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Why not use Enzyme.jl now?

A: Too experimental for production use. GPU support is in active development and requires careful workarounds. ForwardDiff is more reliable.

Q: Is 107ms too slow for a 135k-variable Jacobian?

A: No! This is quite good:

  • Newton converges in 3-5 iterations
  • Total solve time: ~400ms
  • Acceptable for most applications
  • Much faster than dense would be (~hours)

Q: Will GPU autodiff ever be as good as manual Jacobians?

A: Probably not quite, but close enough:

  • Manual GPU Jacobian: ~5ms (estimated)
  • Autodiff on GPU (Reactant): ~10-20ms (projected)
  • Current CPU autodiff: 107ms
  • Manual is 2-4x faster, but requires months of development

Q: Should I wait for Enzyme/Reactant to mature?

A: No, use ForwardDiff now:

  • It works today
  • Performance is acceptable
  • Can migrate later if needed
  • Don't block on experimental technology

Q: What about other packages (ReverseDiff, Diffractor, etc.)?

A:

  • ReverseDiff.jl: Tape-based reverse-mode, no GPU support
  • Diffractor.jl: Experimental, source-to-source AD, not ready
  • Tracker.jl: Deprecated, operator overloading approach
  • None are better than ForwardDiff for this use case

Conclusion

For Powerful.jl in 2025, continue using CPU autodiff with ForwardDiff.jl.

The GPU autodiff ecosystem in Julia is promising but not yet production-ready. ForwardDiff provides excellent performance with rock-solid reliability. When Reactant.jl matures in 1-2 years, it will be worth revisiting this decision.

Key takeaway: Don't let the lack of GPU autodiff block you. The CPU approach is fast enough, and GPU autodiff isn't worth the risk/complexity trade-off in 2025.
